ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals precipitate in joints when serum urate exceeds solubility, causing acute inflammatory arthritis (gout). Diagnosis relies on crystal identification and serum urate levels.

sections.p: Gout is the clinical syndrome caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues. Diagnosis requires finding needle‑shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on polarized microscopy, supported by hyperuricemia.
b: Crystal analysis is the gold standard; serum urate may be normal during an acute attack.

t.a: Joint aspiration with polarized light microscopy
t.b: Does the joint contain MSU crystals? Positive confirms gout; negative does not exclude it if crystals are absent.
Is urate >6.8 mg/dL? Elevated supports gout but can be normal during attacks; repeat after attack if needed.
Are there double‑contour sign or tophi? Helps when aspiration unavailable; may miss early disease.

sections.p: Gout is staged by frequency and joint involvement: intermittent acute attacks, persistent polyarticular disease, and chronic tophaceous gout.
b: Acute: ≤1 joint, <2 weeks.
Polyarticular: >1 joint, recurrent.
Tophaceous: visible or palpable tophi, joint damage.

sections.p: Hyperuricemia results from overproduction or under‑excretion of uric acid. The most common cause is reduced renal clearance, especially in men with obesity, hypertension, or diuretic use.
b: Renal under‑excretion (diuretics, CKD).
Increased production (high purine diet, cell turnover, leukemia).
Genetic defects (renal urate transporters).
Secondary causes in low‑resource settings: HIV therapy, tuberculosis treatment (pyrazinamide), malaria, herbal remedies containing purines.

sections.p: Patients develop sudden, severe joint pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth, classically in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Attacks often awaken patients at night.
b: Pain peaks within 24 h, lasts 3–10 days.
Tophi may appear after years of attacks.

sections.p: Confirm crystal presence, assess urate burden, and rule out mimics.
b: Joint aspiration is essential when diagnosis is uncertain.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis? May suggest infection; normal or mild rise supports gout.
Are kidneys impaired? Guides urate‑lowering drug choice.

sections.p: Uncontrolled gout can lead to joint destruction, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular events.
b: Rapidly enlarging tophus with skin ulceration.
Septic arthritis superimposed on gout.
Acute kidney injury from uric acid nephrolithiasis.

sections.p: Treat the acute flare, then start long‑term urate‑lowering therapy (ULT) to keep serum urate <6 mg/dL.
b: Acute: NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids—choose based on renal function and contraindications.
ULT: Allopurinol or febuxostat—avoid in severe liver disease; start after flare resolves.
Lifestyle: weight loss, limit purine‑rich foods, reduce alcohol.

sections.p: Monitor serum urate every 2–4 weeks after starting ULT until target achieved, then every 6–12 months. Adjust therapy for renal function and adherence.
b: Check for tophi regression.
Re‑educate on diet and medication adherence.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic gout’s acute monoarthritis.
b: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) – positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
Septic arthritis – purulent fluid, positive Gram stain.
Reactive arthritis – follows infection, no crystals.

sections.p: Serum urate may be normal during an acute attack, and inflammation can mask crystal detection.
b: Normal urate does not rule out gout; repeat after attack.
Low‑grade inflammation may yield few crystals; consider repeat aspiration.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading joint swelling, fever, or inability to move the joint – possible septic arthritis.
Severe kidney pain or hematuria – possible uric acid nephrolithiasis.

faq.q: Why can serum urate be normal during an acute gout attack?
faq.a: Inflammation drives urate into tissues, temporarily lowering blood levels.

faq.q: What is the significance of negatively birefringent crystals?
faq.a: They confirm monosodium urate; under polarized light they appear yellow when aligned with the slow axis.

faq.q: When should urate‑lowering therapy be started?
faq.a: After the acute flare resolves and the patient has had ≥2 attacks or has tophi.

exam: Describe the microscopic appearance of monosodium urate crystals and its diagnostic importance.
List the major causes of hyperuricemia and indicate which is most common in low‑resource settings.
Explain the stepwise management of an acute gout flare and the rationale for initiating urate‑lowering therapy.
